analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from using bankruptcy to bury lawsuits over injuries like mesothelioma and opioid harm.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 23, 2024 with bipartisan sponsorship, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change bankruptcy law so companies cannot use chapter 11 to cap or erase lawsuits from people injured by their products — think talc, asbestos, or opioid claims. It lets judges throw out bankruptcy filings that are obviously futile or filed in bad faith, treats a company manufacturing a friendly court venue as evidence of bad faith, and carves certain injury claims out of the automatic stay so victims can still sue parent companies that were stripped of assets. The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People with injury claims against large companies — such as mesothelioma and talc victims, opioid plaintiffs, and other mass-tort claimants — who today can be cut off when the operating company files chapter 11 while the parent keeps the assets. Creditors who are stalled by bankruptcy filings meant to run out the clock also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Lets bankruptcy judges dismiss a chapter 11 case as filed in bad faith or objectively futile, ending multi-year cases whose only purpose is delay or capping liability.
Creates a presumption of bad faith when a company manufactures its bankruptcy venue, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence.

Creates a conclusive presumption of bad faith when a filing caps the debtor's liability to creditors the company can actually pay in full, when the company did a divisional merger or spinoff within four years, or when it has no valid reorganization purpose.

Carves 'protected claims' — injury and contamination claims affecting at least 100 people, plus claims against parent companies, insurers, and restructuring participants — out of the automatic stay, so victims can keep suing non-debtor affiliates even during a bankruptcy.
Bars bankruptcy courts from issuing orders that override that carve-out, closing the route by which nondebtor releases were previously blessed from within a chapter 11 case.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations facing mass injury litigation — pharmaceutical, chemical, and consumer-product companies — along with private equity owners and restructuring specialists who profit from dividing healthy assets away from liability-ridden shells. Their costs go up because injury victims can reach their full assets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mass-tort defendant companies and their owners

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to cases filed or pending on the date of enactment, which raises fairness questions for companies mid-bankruptcy and litigation risk from challenges to the retrospective application.

The conclusive bad-faith presumption and the 100-claimant 'protected claim' definition sweep very broadly — a good-faith critic would say some legitimate reorganizations and lender protections get caught in it, increasing the cost of capital for firms that restructure honestly.

Companies facing mass torts argue that a single consolidated bankruptcy forum can actually pay victims more equitably than a race to the courthouse in scattered state courts; eliminating the stay tool removes that alternative entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the upside is real and targeted: injury victims keep their right to sue well-funded parent companies instead of being funneled into a bankruptcy plan negotiated by the company's own lawyers. The main cost falls on large corporations and their investors through higher litigation exposure, which is the point of the bill. The retroactivity and breadth of the presumptions are genuine design flaws worth fixing, but they do not change who the bill serves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 23, 2024, and the committee never held a hearing or markup on it before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, so it died with no vote anywhere.

narrative.text: Whitehouse introduced the bill for himself, Hawley, and Durbin on July 23, 2024.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day it was introduced.
It attracted two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further steps after the referral; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use chapter 11 filings to cap injury liability and stall creditors keep that playbook intact, and the plaintiffs and creditors it would have helped get nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that bury lawsuits in bankruptcy

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat, a Republican, and a Democrat — but with only two cosponsors and no recorded floor opposition, no party-level split is visible in the record; the bill simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Mass-tort defendant corporations (pharma, talc, chemical, opioid)
industries.note: The bill removes their main tool for capping injury liability through chapter 11: injury claims affecting 100 or more people and claims against parent companies are carved out of the automatic stay, and liability-capping filings can be dismissed as bad faith. Their gain from the bill's failure is victims' continued inability to reach non-debtor assets.

industries.industry: Private equity and corporate restructuring specialists
industries.note: Divisional mergers and spinoffs within four years of filing trigger a conclusive bad-faith presumption, and participants in restructuring transactions become reachable as protected-claim defendants, raising the cost of liability-stripping deal structures.
Claims against insurers that provided coverage to the debtor count as protected claims, so carriers can be pursued directly, but victims of insured harms gain a path to those policy proceeds.
Fewer years-long chapter 11 cases with venue fights and nondebtor-release plans means a smaller fee pool for the professionals who run those cases.
